C debugging roadmap
C basics required: functions, arrays and pointers. Suggested study time: 60 minutes.
1 Workflow
Reproduce symptoms
and check hypotheses
with evidence
2 Isolation
Narrow the cause
across C functions
and source files
3 Tools
Inspect variables,
breakpoints and the C
call stack
4 GDB
Find an off-by-one
loop error and verify
the correction
5 Crashes
Trace a null pointer to
its caller and correct
the cause
By the end: set breakpoints, inspect state, explain a fault and verify a fix. Suggested pace: concepts 15 min,
guided labs 30 min, independent practice and recap 15 min. Use the multi-file lab as extra practice.
The professional debugging loop
Debugging is a controlled experiment, not a guessing game
1
Reproduce
Capture
repeatable steps
where possible.
Keep logs for
intermittent faults.
2
Observe
Collect facts: logs,
stack trace, inputs,
versions.
3
Hypothesize
Hypothesis: "p is
NULL because
init() failed".
4
Test it
Use a breakpoint
or focused probe
to check the
hypothesis.
5
Fix & verify
Correct the cause.
Re-run the failing
case and check
nearby cases.
Common pitfall: changing several things before re-running hides which change mattered. Make one focused
change at a time and record the evidence. If you get stuck, explain the observations to a colleague.
Debugging strategies for modular code
A failure can surface far from the code that introduced the fault
Binary search the pipeline
Inspect data at a midpoint. If a
single bad boundary exists, keep
narrowing the suspect range.
Check that each observation
supports the split.
Trust the boundary, verify the
contract
Verify buffer bounds, object
lifetime and ownership at each
boundary. A non-NULL pointer
alone does not prove that a
dereference is safe.
Shrink the input
Cut the failing payload down
until removing one more field
makes the bug vanish. That field
is your lead.
Isolate with a harness
Call the suspect C function from
a small test executable. Link only
its dependencies to isolate the
failure.
Compare a good and bad run
Compare the same input on a
known good and bad revision.
Use git bisect with a repeatable
pass/fail check to narrow the
introducing commit.
Change one thing at a time
Two simultaneous edits and you
can no longer attribute the
result. Discipline beats speed.
Breakpoints and variable inspection
Stop guessing what the value is —go and look at it
•Line breakpoint: break sum.c:5 stops at the executable code
for that source line, before the addition.
•Conditional breakpoint: break sum.c:5 if i == 1 stops when
the condition is true.
•Watchpoint: watch total stops when the expression value
changes.
•Signal stop: GDB normally stops on SIGSEGV on Linux.
Inspect the fault and call stack before continuing.
info locals shows locals in the selected frame. print evaluates an expression. backtrace shows the stack. next
steps over calls. step can enter calls with debug information. finish runs until the selected frame returns,
unless another stop occurs.
C example: the discount that vanishes
A case-sensitive string comparison skips a valid customer tier
Illustrative bug: apply_discount(600, "gold") returns 600 instead of the expected 540.
Step
What you do
What it tells you
1. Reproduce
Call apply_discount(600, "gold") in a C test.
Expected 540, actual 600.
2. Breakpoint
In GDB: break apply_discount, then run.
Stops in the pricing.c function.
3. Inspect
print tier shows "gold", but code checks "GOLD".
strcmp compares case
-sensitive text.
4. Trace caller
Use backtrace and up to inspect main().
main passes the parsed tier unchanged.
5. Fix and verify
Normalize case at input. Recheck "gold" and
"GOLD".
Both should return 540 for this input.
C strings: strcmp(a, b) == 0 checks equal text in valid NUL-terminated strings. With pointer operands, == compares
pointers.
Tracing a fault across multiple files
Follow the data, not the code
•Use backtrace, then up to walk from the failing C function to
its caller.
•Search declarations in .h files and implementations in .c files.
•Pass a request ID through C function calls and include it in
logs.
•Sketch which module owns each buffer and when it releases
memory.
•Mark each checked value VERIFIED or SUSPECT.
C example: main.c calls parse_tier() in input.c, then apply_discount() in pricing.c. Inspect the value after
parsing and on entry to pricing. Compare it with the documented case-normalization rule.
Multi-file C lab: source files
Extra practice for the discount example. Save each block under the filename shown.
tier.h
#ifndef TIER_H
#define TIER_H
const char *parse_tier(const char *raw);
int apply_discount(int total,
const char *tier);
#endif
input.c (original)
#include "tier.h"
const char *parse_tier(const char *raw) {
return raw;
}
pricing.c
#include <string.h>
#include "tier.h"
int apply_discount(int total,
const char *tier) {
return strcmp(tier, "GOLD") == 0
? total * 9 / 10 : total;
}
Input contract
This exercise accepts "gold" and "GOLD" as gold-tier
input. Both must yield 540 from a total of 600.
Multi-file C lab: run, inspect and fix
Save main.c, build all three .c files together, then follow the same value across calls.
main.c
#include <stdio.h>
#include "tier.h"
int main(void) {
const char *tier = parse_tier("gold");
int result = apply_discount(600, tier);
printf("gold: %d\n", result);
tier = parse_tier("GOLD");
result = apply_discount(600, tier);
printf("GOLD: %d\n", result);
return 0;
}
Expected before fix: gold: 600, GOLD: 540
After fix: both lines report 540.
Build and inspect
$ gcc -g -O0 -Wall -Wextra \
main.c input.c pricing.c -o discount
$ gdb ./discount
(gdb) break apply_discount
(gdb) run
(gdb) print tier
(gdb) up
Replace input.c, rebuild and run ./discount
#include <string.h>
#include "tier.h"
const char *
parse_tier(const char *raw) {
return strcmp(raw, "gold") == 0
? "GOLD" : raw;
}
Error diagnosis: reading what the system tells you
A stack trace is a free confession —most people never read it
Signal
How to read it
Possible cause
SIGSEGV
Inspect the failing pointer and call stack.
Null or dangling pointer, or an out
-of-
bounds access.
Off
-by-one error
Check array length and loop bounds.
Using i <= n instead of i < n.
Fails on one build
Compare compiler flags and input data.
Undefined behavior, build flags or
platform assumptions.
Intermittent failure
Record timing and shared variable access.
Shared
-state race, lifetime bug or
timing
-dependent input.
Wrong result
Check return values and invariants.
Integer division or ignored error code.
Check C return values. If fopen() returns NULL, report the file error before using the FILE pointer.
Reading a C call stack, line by line
Illustrative GDB output for the crash.c example used later
GDB output or command
What it tells you
What to do next
#0 read_value (p=0x0)
at crash.c:2
The innermost frame reads through p,
which is null.
Open line 2 and inspect p.
#1 main ()
at crash.c:6
main passed ptr to read_value().
Open line 6 in the caller.
(gdb) frame 0
Select the failing function frame.
Use info args to inspect p.
(gdb) up
Move to the caller frame.
Use print ptr to check its value.
(gdb) list
Display nearby source lines.
Find where ptr became NULL.
Frame 0 is the innermost stack frame. Use frame or up to select a frame. Inspect both the faulting access and the
caller.
GDB setup and common roadblocks
Shell commands begin with $. Commands inside GDB begin with (gdb). Do not type either prompt.
Check the tools in your terminal
$ gcc --version
$ gdb --version
$ gcc -g -O0 -Wall sum.c -o sum
$ gdb ./sum
Use the sum.c source shown later. Install GCC, C
development headers and GDB with your Linux
package manager if needed.
Fresh build after every source change
Command not found
Install the missing tool and reopen your terminal.
No debugging symbols
Rebuild every source file with -g. Open that executable.
Source lines do not match
Save the source, rebuild successfully and start a fresh GDB
session.
Variable unavailable
Check the selected frame and scope. Use the -O0 lab
build.
GDB quick reference
Commands separated by / are alternatives. Substitute your filenames and breakpoint numbers.
Purpose
Command
Meaning
Session
gdb ./sum (shell)
Open the executable in GDB
Execution
run / continue
Start again / resume from a stop
Stepping
next / step / finish
Step over / enter / run to return
Breakpoint
break sum / break sum.c:5
Stop in a function or at a source line
Condition
break sum.c:5 if i == 1
Stop when the expression is true
Watch
watch total
Stop when the expression changes
Manage
info breakpoints
List breakpoints and their numbers
Manage
disable 1 / enable 1 / delete 1
Deactivate / reactivate / remove #1
Inspect
print total / info locals
Evaluate a value / show frame locals
Stack
backtrace / frame 0 / up
Show stack / select frame / caller
Source / exit
list / quit
Show source / leave GDB
GDB 1: build a small program with a bug
C on Linux: a reproducible example with an expected total of 60
sum.c (save the code exactly as shown)
#include <stdio.h>
int sum(int *values, int n) {
int total = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
total += values[i];
}
return total;
}
int main(void) {
int values[] = {10, 20, 30};
int result = sum(values, 3);
printf("%d\n", result);
return 0;
}
1 Prepare your environment
Check GCC and GDB using the setup slide.
Save sum.c exactly as shown in a new folder.
2 Compile with debug information
$ gcc -g -O0 -Wall sum.c -o sum
$ ./sum
-g emits debugging information.
-O0 disables most optimizations.
Prompts $ and (gdb) are not typed.
Expected for this input: 30 rather than 60. The loop skips the final element. Use nonnegative n and valid array bounds.
GDB 2: stop, step and inspect
Follow the first iteration and compare each value with your expectation
3 Start GDB and stop in sum()
$ gdb ./sum
(gdb) break sum.c:5
(gdb) run
(gdb) info args
(gdb) print i
(gdb) print total
(gdb) print values[i]
(gdb) next
(gdb) print total
4 Read the state at each stop
Expected observations:
print i 0
print total 0
print values[i] 10
After next, print total gives 10. The addition
has now run. Check the displayed source line
at each stop.
next steps over calls. step can enter calls with debug information. continue resumes until a stop or program exit.
GDB 3: conditional breaks and watchpoints
Stop only on the second iteration, then catch the change to total
5 Begin a fresh GDB session
$ gdb ./sum
(gdb) break sum.c:5 if i == 1
(gdb) run
(gdb) print i
(gdb) print total
(gdb) watch total
(gdb) next
(gdb) print total
(gdb) info breakpoints
6 Interpret the evidence
The breakpoint condition stops at i = 1,
before the addition. Expect total to be 10.
watch total tracks value changes. After next
executes the addition, expect total to be
30.
The loop condition i < n - 1 excludes i = 2
for n = 3.
Start a fresh session with the original source. Line 5 must contain the addition. Watchpoints depend on target support.
GDB 4: fix the loop and verify the result
The corrected loop includes the last element. Check the original case and boundary cases
7 Correct the source and rebuild
Before: for (int i = 0; i < n -1; i++)
After: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
8 Run the corrected program
$ gcc -g -O0 -Wall sum.c -o sum
$ ./sum
60
9 Check the missing iteration
$ gdb ./sum
(gdb) break sum.c:5 if i == 2
(gdb) run
(gdb) print values[i]
Verify n = 0, 1 and 3 with valid inputs. One passing case does not prove correctness for all inputs.
GDB 5: reproduce a crash
A second example: inspect a null pointer at the failing statement
crash.c (a deliberately faulty example)
int read_value(int *p) {
return *p;
}
int main(void) {
int *ptr = 0;
int result = read_value(ptr);
return result;
}
10 Compile and run inside GDB
$ gcc -g -O0 crash.c -o crash
$ gdb ./crash
(gdb) run
On a typical Linux system, GDB stops with
SIGSEGV at return *p.
The initializer 0 makes ptr a null pointer. It
does not point to an int object that the
program may read.
Reading through a null pointer is undefined behavior in C. A SIGSEGV is a common Linux outcome, not a C guarantee.
GDB 6: trace the caller and correct the cause
Use the stack to connect the failing read to the pointer supplied by main
11 Inspect the stopped program
(gdb) backtrace
(gdb) frame 0
(gdb) info args
(gdb) print p
(gdb) up
(gdb) info locals
Typical stack: read_value at frame 0, main at frame 1. p
and ptr are null. In main, result has no initialized value
until the call returns.
12 Supply a valid object in main
int value = 42;
int *ptr = &value;
int result = read_value(ptr);
return result == 42 ? 0 : 1;
Quit GDB, replace the body of main, and rebuild.
Run ./crash, then echo $?. Expected exit status: 0,
with no crash.
A valid pointer must refer to a live object of the right type. If NULL is allowed, define and handle that error explicitly.
Independent practice: the wrong maximum
Spend about 10 minutes on this task before viewing the answer.
max.c (save exactly as shown)
int maximum(const int *a, int n) {
int best = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
if (a[i] > best)
best = a[i];
}
return best;
}
int main(void) {
int a[] = {-8, -2, -5};
int result = maximum(a, 3);
return result == -2 ? 0 : 1;
}
Your task
The largest input value is -2.
Find the first state that conflicts with this
expectation. Record a command and its
observed value.
Explain the cause, change the code and verify
the result.
Contract: n >= 1. The array contains at least n valid
int elements.
Build: gcc -g -O0 -Wall -Wextra max.c -o max Start: gdb ./max
Practice answer: initialize from the data
A starting value of zero prevents every negative element from replacing best.
Evidence in the original program
(gdb) break max.c:4
(gdb) run
(gdb) print i
$1 = 0
(gdb) print best
$2 = 0
(gdb) print a[i]
$3 = -8
Expected output shown. GDB result numbers may differ.
Every input is below zero, so the original code never
updates best.
Correction
int best = a[0];
for (int i = 1; i < n; ++i) {
if (a[i] > best)
best = a[i];
}
Replace the initialization and loop only. Keep return best.
Rebuild, run ./max, then echo $?. Expected status: 0.
Also check: {-4} gives -4 and {3, 9, 1} gives 9. Adjust n and
the expected value in main for each case.
A debugging checklist for your next C fault
Completion check: explain the cause from evidence, then verify a focused correction.
01 Reproduce Keep the smallest failing input and record the build.
02 Inspect Stop near the fault. Examine values and the selected stack frame.
03 Explain Connect the incorrect state to the statement or caller that caused it.
04 Correct Make one focused change and rebuild the program.
05 Verify Re-run the original case and relevant boundary cases.
Ready to move on: you can repeat this process on the independent exercise without copying the answer.
